title: The mic hears the neighbours
allegory: Interference is five singers crowded onto a small stage with one directional mic: aim it at one singer and you still hear the neighbours, in proportion to how close they stand, unless they are silent or a noise gate mutes them.
map: five singers on a stage built for two
five features stored as directions in a 2-D hidden space
aiming the directional mic at one singer
reading feature i with its direction w_i (the Wᵀ in WᵀWx)
interference: (w_i · w_j) times feature j's value
singers who rarely sing at the same time
sparsity: features seldom active together, so the leak is rarely paid
a noise gate that mutes anything below a threshold
ReLU plus a negative bias: negative and small leaks are cut to zero

cap.1: The model wants to keep track of five things but has room for only two directions. Something has to give: drop three, or let them overlap.
cap.2: Toy Models of Superposition squeezes 5 features into a 2-D hidden space and back out. With sparse data it keeps all five as overlapping directions, and pays a price.
cap.3: n features in d < n dimensions cannot all be orthogonal. The ReLU output model ReLU(WᵀWx + b) trades representing more features against the cross-terms overlap creates.

cap.1: Picture five singers on a small stage and one directional mic. Aim it at one singer and you still hear the neighbours, quieter the further round they stand.
cap.2: Reading feature i means a dot product with its direction w_i. If feature j is also on, you pick up w_i · w_j times j's value. That leak is interference.
cap.3: Output i = ReLU(Σⱼ (w_i · w_j) xⱼ + bᵢ). The diagonal term reconstructs xᵢ; the off-diagonal terms (w_i · w_j) xⱼ with j ≠ i are interference.

cap.1: Each output is the singer you want, plus every neighbour times how much their direction overlaps yours, then a gate that mutes anything too quiet.
cap.2: Output i is ReLU(|wᵢ|²xᵢ + Σ over j≠i of wᵢ·wⱼ xⱼ + bᵢ). Orthogonal directions would make every leak zero, but five directions can't be orthogonal in 2-D.
cap.3: WᵀW is the Gram matrix; its off-diagonal entries are the interference weights. calculate_loss is an importance-weighted squared error, so leaks into important features cost more.

cap.1: Leaks only matter when two singers sing at once. If each sings one song in ten, two sing together only about one song in a hundred. Rare overlap, cheap leaks.
cap.2: Features are independent, each on with probability p, so two together is p². As data gets sparser, the leak cost falls much faster than the value of storing a feature.
cap.3: Expected interference scales with co-occurrence (p² for independent features), benefit with p. Sparse data makes superposition pay; dense data gives PCA-like behaviour.

chapters.name: Negative leaks are free
chapters.verdict: The ReLU forgives negative interference, not positive.

cap.1: The gate mutes anything below its threshold. A neighbour who comes through 'negative' is muted for free; one who comes through positive sets off a false alarm.
cap.2: If w_i · w_j < 0, feature j pushes output i below zero and ReLU erases it. Positive overlaps survive unless a negative bias cuts them, which also shrinks weak true signals.
cap.3: ReLU makes interference asymmetric: negative cross-terms are free, positive ones cost unless b ≤ −w_i·w_j. That is why antipodal pairs are so cheap.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Steer one feature, nudge its neighbours

cap.1: Models cram in more ideas than they have room for, so ideas overlap. That is why one part can mean several things, and why pushing one idea nudges others.
cap.2: Interference is the price of superposition. It is why single neurons are a poor unit of analysis, why sparse autoencoders exist, and one reason steering along a direction has side effects.
cap.3: Adding α·w_i shifts every overlapping feature's readout by α·(w_i·w_j). Understanding interference is prerequisite to reading features cleanly and to steering without collateral effects.

caption.1: Overlap starts at 0.31, the leak between pentagon neighbours: red sits above the ideal. Pull the gate down until the false signal hits 0. Then try overlap −1.
caption.2: Feature i reads ReLU(xᵢ + overlap + bias) while its neighbour sings. A negative bias gates small positive leaks, but look at the green line: weak true signals shrink too.
caption.3: Antipodal (overlap −1) is free under ReLU; a positive overlap needs b ≤ −w_i·w_j, costing |b| on every true activation. The geometry trades packing against overlap.

where_else: Polysemantic neurons: one neuron responding to several unrelated things
Sparse autoencoders: learning many directions to pull superposed features apart
Steering side effects: pushing one direction also nudges features that overlap it
Crosstalk and compressed sensing: sparse signals sharing too few channels

hamming.what: The leak between features stored as overlapping directions: reading one picks up a bit of every feature it overlaps with.
hamming.when: Whenever a network stores more features than it has dimensions, which superposition says is normal when features are sparse.
hamming.why: It is the price of superposition, and its shape (free when negative, cheap when sparse) explains the geometry models choose and the side effects of steering.

object.title: The crosstalk desk
object.subtitle: A mixing desk for five singers stored as a pentagon in 2-D: row = whose mic, column = who is singing, height = how loud they come through the gate.

cap.1: A mixing desk for five singers. Row is whose mic, column is who is singing, height is how loud they come through.
cap.2: Bar (r, c) = ReLU(w_r·w_c + b) for five features in a pentagon in 2-D; the diagonal is each feature reading itself.
cap.3: The gated Gram matrix of a pentagon embedding: cos 72° ≈ 0.31 survives the ReLU; cos 144° ≈ −0.81 does not.

cap.1: Next-door singers leak in at about a third. Singers across the stage come through below zero, so the gate removes them completely.
cap.2: Adjacent features overlap +0.31 and leak through; non-adjacent ones overlap −0.81 and ReLU zeroes them.
cap.3: Negative interference is free under ReLU, which is why wide-angle and antipodal arrangements are cheap.

cap.1: Lower the gate a little: the neighbour leaks shrink, and so does each singer's own signal.
cap.2: Bias −0.2 cuts the adjacent leak to 0.11, but every true reading of 1 now comes out as 0.8.
cap.3: The bias trades false positives against shrinkage of true activations: it removes interference smaller than |b|.

cap.1: At about −0.31 the leaks vanish. The price: every true signal now comes through at 0.69.
cap.2: b ≤ −0.31 gates a single neighbour's leak; the diagonal shrinks to 1 + b.
cap.3: This suppresses single-neighbour interference only: two adjacent features firing together leak 2 × 0.31 = 0.62, which clears the gate. Sparsity keeps that rare.

predict.q: Two features point in exactly opposite directions. A fires alone. What does B read after the ReLU?

options.t: Zero: the leak is negative and the ReLU cuts it

predict.why: B reads w_B·w_A × x_A = −x_A, which is negative, so the ReLU sets it to zero. Antipodal pairs cost nothing.

predict.q: Features become sparser (each fires less often). What happens to the interference cost?

options.t: It falls fast: overlapping features rarely fire together
It stays the same: the directions haven't changed

predict.why: Leaks only cost when two features are on together. For independent features that chance is p², which falls faster than p.

predict.q: Why can't the five features all be orthogonal here?

options.t: 2-D has room for only two orthogonal directions
Training forgot to make them orthogonal

predict.why: In d dimensions at most d directions can be mutually orthogonal, so the other three must overlap someone.

object.where: Any shared channel: crosstalk between phone lines, stations bleeding into each other, compressed sensing.
